news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh's mid-year treasury report lists 12 LOBO loans totalling £122.4m, with rates of 4.375% to 5.25%
news_drafts.lead:
City of Edinburgh Council had 12 LOBO loans outstanding at 30 September 2026, with a combined principal of £122.4m. A LOBO loan is a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher interest rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it. The figures are in the Treasury Mid-Term Report 2026-2027, which goes to the Finance and Resources Committee on 17 November.

The debt table in the report's Appendix 4 sets out each loan's principal, rate and maturity. Coupons on the 12 loans run from 4.375% to 5.25%. Maturities run from 2028 to 2066.

The paper does not describe any lender call, repayment or replacement of the loans. The table shows them as outstanding at the date of the report, and the council has reported them as listed rather than as a repayment event.

news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh's plan shows a £14.3m gap for 2027/28, rising to £93.0m cumulatively by 2030/31
news_drafts.lead:
The City of Edinburgh Council's medium-term financial plan forecasts a budget shortfall of £14.3m in 2027/28. The cumulative funding gap, excluding the Edinburgh Integration Joint Board (EIJB), which runs health and social care, rises to £47.3m in 2028/29, £70.8m in 2029/30 and £93.0m by 2030/31. The council's update to the plan, set out in February 2026, is in the papers for its meeting on 29 October.

A budget strategy progress update restates the 2027/28 gap from the June 2026 update. It says projections for later years are unchanged pending the Scottish Budget. The gap includes additional sums set aside for contract and other non-pay inflation, and the paper says there remains a risk around the adequacy of that provision. The council's external auditor says the council has developed medium and longer-term financial plans and that the plan shows it is financially sustainable in the short term. Its Exhibit 7 states: "There remain significant risks around long-term borrowing and funding gaps".

The council's share of the EIJB's projected gaps is shown separately: £19.7m in 2027/28, rising to £91.4m in 2030/31. Combined with the council's own gap, the total reaches £184.4m in 2030/31. The council's baseline planning assumption is that "the EIJB will address its own budget gaps without additional" council funding. It does not consider the EIJB's future pressures when developing savings plans, but says it will monitor any risk of overspend that could require additional council funding.
news_drafts.paper_title: Item 7.4 - The City of Edinburgh Council – 2025-26 Annual Audit Report - Appendix 1

news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh: £4m empty-home premium for housing would raise 2027/28 funding gap from £14.3m to £18.3m
news_drafts.lead:
Dedicating £4m of new council tax income from second and long-term empty homes to housing projects would raise the City of Edinburgh Council's funding gap for 2027/28 from £14.3m to £18.3m. That is according to a report to its Policy and Sustainability Committee, which met on 20 October 2026. The gap is the further savings the council has still to find for that year, which the report calls its "incremental funding gap".

The money comes from the premium, an extra charge added to council tax on those homes. The report says the council had already assumed the new premium income when it set its 2026/27 budget, and estimates it at £4m in 2027/28. Dedicating it to new housing spending means it is not available to close the gap, which widens by the full £4m.

The report's wording is that "introducing new commitments in the way suggested in the motion would add up to £4m to the Council's incremental funding gap in 2027/28". The paper is headed "Application of Second and Long-Term Empty Home Council Tax Premium Income".
news_drafts.paper_title: 7.6 - Application of Second and Long-Term Empty Home Council Tax Premium Income

findings.headline: The EADP Adult Community Treatment Services contract, £15,069,360, ends 31/12/2026; a separate Adult Alcohol and Drugs Treatment Services renewal of £5m and above is forecast for committee approval in Mar-27.
findings.detail: Appendix 2 lists the Edinburgh Alcohol and Drugs Partnership (EADP) Adult Community Treatment Services contract with an end date of 31/12/2026 and a value of £15,069,360. Appendix 1 lists an Adult Alcohol and Drugs Treatment Services renewal (£5m and above) with forecast approval in Mar-27, which is marked "In tender phase." The paper does not state whether these two items are the same service.
findings.matters: A contract of this size ending about three months before its forecast replacement approval is a timing gap that finance directors and lenders would want to see confirmed or explained.
findings.figures: £15,069,360 contract value; end date 31/12/2026; forecast approval Mar-27

findings.headline: Roads and Transport Infrastructure Construction Framework 2022-2026, £101,760,000, ends 04/04/2027; the paper lists a Roads & Infrastructure multi-lot framework renewal forecast for committee approval in May-27.
findings.detail: Appendix 2 lists the Roads and Transport Infrastructure Construction Framework with an end date of 04/04/2027. Appendix 1 lists a "Roads & Infrastructure" renewal, a multi-lot framework, with forecast committee approval in May-27 and the status "Strategy Development." The paper does not state that these two items are linked.
findings.matters: A framework of this size ending before its forecast replacement is approved is a timing point that finance officers at other councils with similar framework arrangements would compare against their own.
findings.figures: £101,760,000 contract value; end date 04/04/2027; forecast approval May-27

findings.headline: Homelessness Welcome Centre Service (more than £5m, renewal) has an extension option to 31/3/27, with committee approval forecast Mar-27 and tender documentation still being developed.
findings.detail: The paper says the service "Has extension option up to 31/3/27." The forecast approval date for the renewal is Mar-27, the same month the extension option ends. The paper says tender documentation is being developed.
findings.matters: When the forecast approval date falls in the same month as the last extension date, a finance director would want to know what happens to the service if the replacement is not in place by then.
findings.figures: More than £5m estimated value; extension option up to 31/3/27; forecast approval Mar-27

findings.headline: Third Sector Income Maximisation, Welfare and Debt Advice Service (more than £5m, new) has grant funding ending 31/4/27, with committee approval forecast Mar-27 and the contract out to market.
findings.detail: Appendix 1 lists this as a new contract with forecast committee approval in Mar-27. The paper's note reads "Grant funding ends 31/4/27. Out to market." The date is written as 31/4/27 in the paper, which is not a valid date for April.
findings.matters: A service funded by a grant that ends before its replacement contract is approved shows a funding gap that finance officers at this council and at peer councils would need to plan for.
findings.figures: More than £5m estimated value; grant funding ends 31/4/27; forecast approval Mar-27

findings.headline: Usher Hall performed ahead of its 2025/26 target, allowing the wider Cultural Venues service to present a balanced budget
findings.detail: The paper reports a 2025/26 venues income target of £4.7 million, excluding gross ticket sales, equal to 92% of budgeted cost turnover. It says the Usher Hall was ahead of target, which allowed the wider service to balance its budget for the year.
findings.matters: A venue that exceeds its income target and carries a service to balance is a useful outturn reference for finance officers at other councils with similar venue income lines.
findings.figures: £4.7 million income target excluding gross ticket sales; 92% of budgeted cost turnover
findings.quote: The Usher Hall performed ahead of target, allowing the wider service to present a balanced budget for the year.
